'''Alfred Benninghoven''' (8 February 1932 in [[Frankfurt]] -  22 December 2017<ref>{{cite web|url=http://lebenswege.faz.net/traueranzeige/prof-dr-rer-nat-alfred-benninghoven/52357787|title=Prof. Dr. rer. nat. Alfred Benninghoven: Traueranzeige|work=Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung|date=2017-12-30|access-date=2017-12-30}}</ref>) was a German physicist and mass spectrometry researcher known for his work on [[static secondary ion mass spectrometry]].<ref name="encyclopedia">{{cite book |doi=10.1016/B978-0-08-100379-4.00053-8 |chapter=Alfred Benninghoven |title=The Encyclopedia of Mass Spectrometry |year=2015 |last1=Jane Gale |first1=P. |pages=15–16 |isbn=978-0-08-100379-4 }}</ref>

==Career and Research==
Benninghoven graduated from the [[University of Cologne]] in 1961 where he worked with [[Fritz Kirchner]] (1896–1967) and completed his [[habilitation]] in surface physics in Cologne two years later.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> He first worked as professor in Cologne from 1965 to 1973 until he moved to a full professor position in experimental physics at the [[University of Münster]] in 1972.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> He worked on [[static secondary ion mass spectrometry]] (SIMS) and its applications, and developed SIMS instruments. In 1989 he co-founded [[IonTOF]], a company that became a world-leader in [[Time-of-flight mass spectrometry|TOF]]-SIMS instrumentation.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> He has written over 300 scientific articles and several books on the topic of SIMS, many of which have become reference works on SIMS.<ref name="encyclopedia"/>

For his work, he has received the Technology Transfer prize (German Ministry of Education and Research) and the 1984 Gaede-Langmuir Prize (American Vacuum Society) for ''the development of concepts and instrumentation in static secondary ion mass spectrometry and the demonstration of its usefulness in manifold applications''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www2.avs.org/historybook/links/glwincit.htm|title = Winners of the Gaede-Langmuir Award}}</ref> In 1990 he shared the Fritz-Pregl-Medaille of the Austrian Society of Analytical Chemistry with Wilhelm Simon. From 1977 to 1983, he was president of the German Vacuum Society (part of the German Physical Society).
